sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in Jackson County, Missouri: Downtown Kansas City
National Register of Historic Places listings in Jackson County, Missouri

stops.name: New York Life Building
stops.description: Kansas City's first skyscraper, finished in 1889 with the city's first elevators, and still watched over by Louis Saint-Gaudens's bronze eagle above the Ninth Street door.

stops.name: Savoy Hotel and Grill
stops.description: Open since 1888 and once the longest continuously running hotel west of the Mississippi, it closed in 2016 for a fifty million dollar overhaul and reopened two years later.

stops.name: Scarritt Building and Arcade
stops.description: A 1906 Chicago-style office block by Root and Siemens, whose shopping arcade gives the Walnut Street half of the building its own address.

stops.name: Central Library
stops.description: The main library moved into a former bank here, and its parking garage wears book spines roughly 25 feet tall, the titles picked by Kansas City readers.

stops.name: Boley Building
stops.description: Louis Curtiss hung glass on a steel frame here in 1909, one of the first curtain walls anywhere and the first to use rolled-steel columns.

stops.name: Oppenstein Brothers Memorial Park
stops.description: A pocket park on the northeast corner of 12th and Walnut, rebuilt in 2008 around a design called Celestial Flyways.

stops.name: Hotel Phillips
stops.description: A 1931 Art Deco hotel whose lobby holds an eleven-foot Goddess of Dawn carved the same year by local sculptor Jorgen Dreyer.

stops.name: Folly Theater
stops.description: Kansas City's oldest surviving theater, built in 1900 for vaudeville, later a burlesque house, and now a jazz and concert stage.

stops.name: Midland Theatre
stops.description: A 1927 Loew's movie palace fitted out with five hand-cut Czechoslovak crystal chandeliers and over 500,000 feet of gold leaf.

stops.name: Kansas City Club Building
stops.description: A 14-story Gothic Revival tower raised between 1918 and 1922 as a private gentlemen's clubhouse, which it stayed until 2001.

stops.name: Kansas City Power and Light Building
stops.description: This 34-story Art Deco tower was the tallest building west of the Mississippi until the Space Needle, and its lantern still glows red-orange every evening.

stops.name: Municipal Auditorium
stops.description: A 1935 Streamline Moderne hall that hosted three of the first four NCAA basketball Final Fours.

stops.name: Kauffman Center for the Performing Arts
stops.description: Moshe Safdie's 2011 hall behind a curved glass front, holding the city's symphony in one auditorium and its ballet and opera in the other.

stops.name: Kansas City Union Station
stops.description: A 1914 Beaux-Arts terminal with a 95-foot Grand Hall ceiling and three chandeliers of 3,500 pounds each, and the site out front of the 1933 Kansas City Massacre.

stops.name: National World War I Museum and Memorial
stops.description: America's official World War I museum sits beneath a 217-foot tower that burns a lit steam flame at its top after dark.

note: Kansas City, MO is the first city on the NFL slate that has never had a run; the rotation has gone alphabetically through Jacksonville. 15 stops verified, all from English Wikipedia articles carrying coordinates, and all but one with a street address confirmed against the NRHP downtown Kansas City listing or the article's own infobox. ZIPs were looked up per stop and every address resolved. Two things a human should know. First, Oppenstein Brothers Memorial Park has no street number in any source I could verify (the article gives only the northeast corner of 12th and Walnut), so its address and zip are left null rather than guessed; it does carry coordinates. Second, the Central Library article's own coordinate points at 500 E 9th St, the stale NRIS address for the 1895 building, not at 14 W 10th St where the library actually stands, so the coordinate here comes from the Kansas City Public Library article, which pins the same building correctly. On shape: stops 1 through 12 form roughly a 1-mile loop through the Library District, the financial core and the Power and Light District, then the Kauffman Center, Union Station and the WWI Memorial run about 0.6 miles further south along the streetcar line, so the full walk is nearer 1.6 miles end to end. Dropped from the sweep: the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse and the Kansas City Massacre (events, not places), Louis Curtiss Studio Building and several NRHP rows whose listed address is a range rather than a number, the Muehlebach Hotel (standing as a wing of the Marriott but I could not verify its street number from an independent source), and Mainstreet Theatre, which sits a block from the Midland and would have made the theater run repetitive.
